subject: Archaeology
title: ISIS and the Destruction of Nimrud
description: A quick win: understand ISIS and the Destruction of Nimrud.

hook.text: In 2015, ISIS bulldozed the 3,000-year-old Assyrian city of Nimrud and released a video of militants smashing winged bull statues.

buildup.text: ISIS declared pre-Islamic artifacts idolatrous and systematically destroyed sites across Iraq and Syria.

discovery.text: Palmyra, Hatra, Nineveh's gates, and Jonah's Mosque were all damaged or destroyed. Mosul Museum was ransacked on camera.

twist.text: While publicly destroying large pieces, ISIS secretly sold smaller portable artifacts on the black market to fund its operations.

climax.text: After ISIS was expelled, archaeologists returned to find some damage was less severe than feared.

punchline.text: They smashed ancient art for cameras and sold the small pieces for cash.

quiz.question: What was ISIS's dual approach to Mesopotamian artifacts?
options: They destroyed everything equally regardless of size or value
They publicly destroyed large pieces for propaganda while selling smaller ones for profit
They relocated artifacts to museums in allied countries for safekeeping

details.summary: ISIS systematically destroyed ancient Assyrian sites including Nimrud and Nineveh between 2014 and 2017, bulldozing and dynamiting irreplaceable monuments. These acts of cultural destruction were filmed and distributed as propaganda, targeting heritage as an act of ideological warfare.
details.whyItMatters: The destruction of Nimrud showed that cultural heritage remains a target in modern conflicts. It accelerated global efforts to protect archaeological sites during warfare and to digitally preserve threatened heritage.
takeaways: ISIS destroyed Nimrud and other Assyrian sites from 2014 to 2017
Destruction was filmed as propaganda and ideological warfare
It spurred global digital preservation and heritage protection efforts

faq.question: Why did ISIS destroy ancient sites?
faq.answer: ISIS claimed religious justification, calling pre-Islamic artifacts idolatrous. However, they also looted and sold artifacts for profit. The filmed destruction served as propaganda to demonstrate ideological power and provoke international outrage, amplifying their media presence.

faq.question: Can the destroyed sites be restored?
faq.answer: Some partial restoration is possible using 3D scans, photographs, and salvaged fragments. Iraqi archaeologists are leading reconstruction efforts at Nimrud. However, the original ancient fabric is permanently lost — reconstructions are modern recreations, not authentic monuments.
